items.prompt:
(1) Which description fits an electrode in an electrolytic cell?
A. An ionic liquid carrying charge between electrodes
B. An ion moving through the conducting solution
C. A separator preventing products from mixing
D. A conductor contacting the electrolyte [1]

(2) Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
A. Its ions can move and carry charge
B. Electrons move freely through the liquid salt
C. Neutral sodium atoms carry the current
D. Melting removes the charges from the ions [1]

(3) Which process defines the anode in electrolysis?
A. Electron gain at the positive electrode
B. Electron gain at the negative electrode
C. Electron loss at the negative electrode
D. Electron loss at the positive electrode [1]

(4) Which arrangement is suitable for an electrolytic cell?
A. Touching immersed electrodes across a DC supply
B. Separated immersed electrodes across a DC supply
C. Separated dry electrodes above the electrolyte
D. Separated immersed electrodes with no external connection [1]

(5) Which half-equation represents reduction of copper(II) ions?
A. Cu + 2e⁻ → Cu²⁺
B. Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻
C. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
D. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu [1]

(6) Which products form from molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: bromine
B. Cathode: lead; anode: oxygen
C. Cathode: lead; anode: bromine
D. Cathode: bromine; anode: lead [1]

(7) Why does dilute sulfuric acid give twice as much hydrogen as oxygen by volume during electrolysis with inert electrodes, at equal gas conditions?
A. Hydrogen molecules have twice oxygen’s volume at equal moles
B. The overall change is 2H2O → 2H2 + O2
C. The hydrogen electrode receives twice the current
D. Oxygen atoms carry twice as many hydrogen atoms [1]

(8) Which products form during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous hydrochloric acid with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine
B. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen
C. Cathode: chlorine; anode: hydrogen
D. Cathode: hydrogen chloride; anode: chlorine [1]

(9) A molten binary salt contains Li⁺ and Br⁻ ions. Which products are predicted with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: bromine
B. Cathode: lithium; anode: oxygen
C. Cathode: lithium; anode: bromine
D. Cathode: bromine; anode: lithium [1]

(10) Which anode change occurs during electrolysis of aqueous CuSO4 with copper electrodes?
A. Copper ions gain electrons there
B. Copper atoms gain two electrons
C. Copper atoms dissolve as Cu²⁺
D. Water oxidises instead of copper [1]

(11) Which is a use of electroplating?
A. Mixing metals into bulk alloys
B. Applying a decorative metal coating
C. Removing a metal by dissolution
D. Filtering out dissolved metal ions [1]

(12) Why is molten cryolite used with pure aluminium oxide in aluminium manufacture?
A. It dissolves oxide at a lower temperature
B. It reduces the oxide instead of electrical current
C. It supplies most of the extracted aluminium
D. It raises the oxide’s required operating temperature [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) D. A conductor contacting the electrolyte. An electrode carries electrons to or from the reaction boundary.
Distractor explanations: A: This describes the electrolyte, not an electrode. B: An ion is a charge carrier, not the external conductor. C: A separator is not the conductor transferring electrons at the electrolyte boundary.

(2) A. Its ions can move and carry charge. Melting releases ions from fixed lattice positions.
Distractor explanations: B: Charge passes through molten salt by ions, not free electrons. C: The mobile carriers are charged ions, not neutral atoms. D: Melting frees ions to move; it does not remove their charges.

(3) D. Electron loss at the positive electrode. Oxidation, loss of electrons, occurs at the anode.
Distractor explanations: A: The anode loses electrons; electron gain is reduction. B: This describes cathodic reduction. C: In an electrolytic cell the anode is positive, not negative.

(4) B. Separated immersed electrodes across a DC supply. The external circuit and mobile ions provide a complete path through separated electrodes.
Distractor explanations: A: Touching electrodes can short-circuit the supply. C: Electrodes must contact the electrolyte to transfer charge. D: Electrolysis requires an external source and complete circuit.

(5) D. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu Copper ions gain two electrons, balancing charge.
Distractor explanations: A: Adding electrons cannot produce a positive ion from a neutral atom; charge is unbalanced. B: Reduction consumes electrons; this places them on the wrong side. C: This is oxidation of copper, the reverse process.

(6) C. Cathode: lead; anode: bromine. Pb²⁺ gains electrons and Br⁻ loses electrons.
Distractor explanations: A: The molten salt contains no water or hydrogen ions to produce hydrogen. B: The molten bromide supplies bromide ions, not an oxygen source. D: Lead forms at the cathode and bromine at the anode; these are reversed.

(7) B. The overall change is 2H2O → 2H2 + O2. The balanced overall equation gives a 2:1 gas amount ratio.
Distractor explanations: A: Equal gas amounts occupy equal volumes at the same conditions. C: The same current passes through both electrodes in the circuit. D: The volume ratio follows the balanced reaction, not this atomic description.

(8) A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine. Hydrogen ions gain electrons and chloride ions lose electrons under these conditions.
Distractor explanations: B: Concentrated chloride solution produces chlorine at the inert anode under the stated conditions. C: This reverses the cathode and anode products. D: Hydrogen ions are reduced to hydrogen, not hydrogen chloride.

(9) C. Cathode: lithium; anode: bromine. Apply cation reduction and anion oxidation to the specified water-free melt.
Distractor explanations: A: There is no water or hydrogen source in the specified molten salt. B: There is no oxygen-containing ion in the binary salt. D: Lithium is reduced at the cathode; bromide is oxidised at the anode.

(10) C. Copper atoms dissolve as Cu²⁺. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. This applies to an active copper anode.
Distractor explanations: A: Copper ions gain electrons at the cathode, not the anode. B: Copper atoms lose electrons at the anode. D: An active copper anode dissolves instead of the inert-anode water-oxidation route.

(11) B. Applying a decorative metal coating. Electroplating deposits a metal coating on a conducting object.
Distractor explanations: A: Bulk alloy formation is not deposition of a surface coating. C: Electroplating deposits metal on an object rather than simply removing it. D: Dissolved ions pass through ordinary filters; electroplating uses electrode reduction.

(12) A. It dissolves oxide at a lower temperature. The conducting molten mixture permits electrolysis at a lower temperature.
Distractor explanations: B: Electrical reduction still releases the aluminium; cryolite is not the reducing agent. C: The aluminium oxide feed supplies the extracted metal. D: Cryolite lowers the required operating temperature rather than raising it.

(d) Explain how replacing the copper anode with inert carbon changes the anode product and the blue colour of aqueous copper(II) sulfate during continued electrolysis. The cathode remains copper. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Reduction.

(b) Hydrogen forms at the negative cathode; chlorine forms at the positive anode.

(c) With an active copper anode in aqueous CuSO4, copper atoms leave the anode as dissolved Cu²⁺ ions by losing two electrons each: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.

(d) Replacing the active copper anode with inert carbon in aqueous CuSO4 gives oxygen at the carbon anode instead of copper dissolving. Cu²⁺ still gains electrons and deposits at the cathode. These removed ions are no longer replenished by the anode, so the blue colour fades as their concentration decreases.
marking_guidance: Part a: Reduction (1).
Part b: Hydrogen at cathode (1).
Part b: Chlorine at anode (1).
Part c: Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺ (1).
Part c: Loss of two electrons per copper atom (1).
Part d: Oxygen replaces copper dissolution at anode (1).
Part d: Cu²⁺ continues to deposit as copper at cathode (1).
Part d: No anode replenishment, so Cu²⁺ concentration and blue colour decrease (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Draw a labelled arrangement for teacher-supervised electrolysis of aqueous CuSO4 using separated carbon electrodes and a low-voltage DC supply. Include an inverted, initially water-filled tube to collect a small gas sample above the positive electrode. Keep the cell open to the atmosphere. [3]

(b) Describe how to collect a small uncontaminated sample of the gas from the carbon anode in aqueous CuSO4, and test it for oxygen, including the positive observation. The teacher handles the powered apparatus. [3]

(c) Deduce the identity of a gas that relights a glowing splint. This observation is from a classroom observation record for aqueous CuSO4 electrolysis using carbon electrodes. [1]

(d) Explain how charge is carried through the aqueous electrolyte and through the external metal leads in this cell. [2]

(e) Plan a teacher-supervised comparison of carbon and copper anodes in aqueous CuSO4. Include a fair comparison, electrode-mass measurements, a gas test and a conclusion method. Both trials have copper cathodes and a low-voltage current-controlled supply. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The DC positive lead connects to a carbon anode and the negative lead to a separate carbon cathode. Both dip into aqueous CuSO4 without touching. An inverted water-filled tube has its submerged open mouth over the anode so bubbles displace water; the connecting lead enters through the open mouth, not through glass. The beaker remains open.

(b) Fill and invert a collection tube under water so it starts without an air pocket, position its submerged mouth above the carbon anode, and collect a small gas sample by water displacement. After the teacher disconnects the supply, test the sample with a glowing splint; oxygen relights it.

(c) Oxygen.

(d) Mobile positive and negative ions transport charge through the electrolyte. Electrons transport charge through the external metal leads; electrons are transferred at the electrode surfaces.

(e) Compare a carbon anode with a copper anode, using a copper cathode in each fresh CuSO4 sample. Keep solution concentration and volume, immersed electrode area and temperature the same. Set equal measured current for equal time. Clean, rinse and dry electrodes consistently and weigh before and after each run. Collect any anode gas separately and test with a glowing splint after disconnecting. Compare anode mass change and gas observations: a copper anode should lose mass while a carbon anode produces oxygen; both cathodes gain copper. Repeat to check consistency.
marking_guidance: Part a: DC supply with positive anode and negative cathode (1).
Part a: Separated electrodes immersed in named electrolyte (1).
Part a: Workable gas collection above anode with open submerged mouth and no sealed cell (1).
Part b: Collection without an initial air pocket or mixing with the other electrode gas (1).
Part b: Glowing splint test (1).
Part b: Splint relights (1).
Part c: Oxygen (1).
Part d: Mobile ions carry charge in electrolyte (1).
Part d: Electrons carry charge in external leads (1).
Part e: Compare carbon and copper anodes explicitly (1).
Part e: Same CuSO4 concentration and volume (1).
Part e: Equal measured current and electrolysis time (1).
Part e: Clean dry electrode masses before and after (1).
Part e: Collect and test anode gas (1).

Part e: Compare mass changes and products to conclude effect of anode material (1). Accept equivalent controlled apparatus; do not substitute voltage alone for controlled current. No extra marks beyond six.

items.prompt: Define an electrolyte in terms of charge transport and chemical change.
items.canonical_answer: An electrolyte is a substance that conducts by moving ions when molten or in solution and undergoes chemical decomposition during electrolysis.
marking_guidance: Conduction by mobile ions in molten or dissolved state (1).
Chemical decomposition during electrolysis (1).

items.prompt: Distinguish the anode and cathode in an electrolytic cell by polarity and the electron-transfer process.

items.prompt: Construct half-equations for the cathode and anode during electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes.
items.canonical_answer: Cathode: Pb²⁺+2e⁻→Pb. Anode: 2Br⁻→Br2+2e⁻.
